archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergrad research since my sophomore year, which has been an eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I initially didn't see myself going down the research route, but after being approached by a professor who saw my potential in bridging technical coding with user experience, I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.

archival_memory.current_lab: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work on making massive datasets more comprehensible. In contrast to the small datasets used in classes, we handle datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. My main task is developing front-end prototypes that present data slices in dynamic, interactive dashboards. I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.

archival_memory.first_project: My first research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific, scattered across different servers. The raw data was enormous, consisting of tons of files, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. My task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent manner to show patterns over months or years. I dove headfirst into the project, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored a paper on this system. Seeing my name in an official publication was surreal, and it remains one of my proudest moments in college.

archival_memory.current_research: My current research has pivoted to immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' intuitive understanding of complex data. It's a leap from coding websites to creating 3D representations that can be interacted with in a virtual environment. The process involves experimentation, integrating VR headsets, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into these environments using engines like Unity or Unreal. It's cutting-edge, and it's exciting to forge my own path as there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.

archival_memory.research_life: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It's a lot of reading, especially when trying to solve a specific problem like rendering volumetric data in VR. I need to comb through conference proceedings and workshops to see if someone has tried something similar. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine relevance. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I share it with the lab and we discuss how to incorporate that technique into our workflow.

archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I interact with a lot of graduate students in the lab, both master's and PhD students. It can be intimidating at first because they're deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and integrating it with our VR platform. The idea is to use a compressed representation of the data until you zoom in. It's a wild but practical approach for real-time performance. Working alongside him allows me to see how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-world scenarios. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room over coffee, where we hash out how to offload processing to the GPU.

archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present at a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience, as it forced me to distill complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries like marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.

archival_memory.publications: I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission to the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS). We're conducting a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than 2D charts. We've completed a small set of user trials with 15 participants, recording their times and gathering UX questionnaires. Now we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with different sections handled by different team members. I'm responsible for the system architecture and prototype design, while others are writing about the user study methodology and our PI is weaving it all together. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.

archival_memory.future_plans: I'm considering working in the industry for a couple of years before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. I'm drawn to the idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts are applied in real product development. One of my mentors suggested that industry experience can provide a better understanding of relevant problems, making my future research more practical. I'm excited to explore both options and see where my path takes me.

archival_memory.frustrations: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your idea has already been done and improved upon by others. It can be disheartening. However, the key is to adapt. We read existing papers, incorporate their findings, and find new angles or applications. Research is about building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special.

archival_memory.server_crash: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we lost some vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a frantic night of email chains and Zoom calls with the lab manager as everyone scrambled to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. Afterward, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we don't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but it also brought the lab together.

archival_memory.research_journey: My research journey so far has been a mix of hard work and chaos, but it's also been incredibly rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in the future. The VR and immersive technologies we're pioneering could become standard tools one day, and I'd be proud to say I was part of that from the beginning. The sense of contributing to something bigger is what motivates me. Whether or not I pursue grad school soon, this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. It's enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
